Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "for a little over two years i have helped with the monthly film nights at the old Marlowe Community Hall, and i still think of them as a small event that keeps turning out to be larger than its room. The hall is on a side street behind the library, with a basement room that holds about forty chairs if we leave the folding tables against the wall. We show one film on the second Friday of each month, usually something that can start at seven and finish before the last bus at 9:42. People bring tea in mismatched mugs, and the projector fan is loud enough that the first few minutes always feel like a test of our patience.

I began going because my neighbor Ruth asked if i could carry a box of programs downstairs. I did not know the other volunteers, and i expected to leave as soon as the box was empty. Instead, i stayed to tape a cable to the floor and then to watch the film. Ruth said, “If you help once, you’ll probably know where everything goes next time.” She was right about the equipment, though not about how quickly i would learn everyone’s names. It took me several months to stop calling Martin “the man with the blue scarf.”

The work has a rhythm, but it is not quite as simple as setting up chairs and pressing play. We have a small group chat for practical matters, and a paper checklist that lives in a drawer beside the kettle. The checklist is useful until somebody moves the extension lead, which happens often enough that we now write its location in pencil. On film nights, people arrive at different times, and each arrival changes what needs doing. I have found it helpful to think about the routine in three parts:

1. Before the doors open, we move the tables, arrange the chairs in uneven rows, and check that the screen is not blocking the fire-exit sign. We test the sound from the back row because dialogue that seems clear beside the laptop can disappear near the door. If the film has subtitles, we dim the lights once and check that the lowest line can still be read over the heads in front. This is often where we discover that a chair has a wobbly leg or that the remote is in someone’s coat pocket.

2. As people come in, we collect the optional £3 donation and point out the tea, the toilets, and the empty seats. We do not reserve places, although Ruth sometimes saves two chairs for people who have rung to say they are coming straight from work. A few people ask whether the film is “the sort where we have to be quiet.” I usually say that people can react naturally, but that we try not to talk over the dialogue. That answer sounds obvious, yet it has helped people who are coming to a film night for the first time.

3. Afterward, we wait until the room has mostly emptied before stacking chairs, coiling cables, and checking under the seats for cups. Some people stay to talk about the film; others head out quickly to catch the bus. We keep the discussion informal and do not ask anyone to share an opinion. The last job is to put the kettle away and make sure the hall door has latched behind us.

The films have been varied, partly because we take suggestions from people who attend and partly because the volunteers do not agree on everything. In March we showed a quiet documentary about a family-run bakery, and the smell of actual toast from the kitchen made the timing seem accidentally perfect. In June we screened a black-and-white comedy that Martin had watched with his father when he was young. He introduced it with a short story, then stood at the back and laughed before anyone else did. One person told us afterward, “I thought I’d feel out of place, but it was like watching something at a friend’s house.” I kept thinking about that sentence while we folded the chairs.

Not every evening goes smoothly. Once the subtitles were out of sync by several seconds, and we paused twice while a volunteer tried to correct them. Another time, the hall heating came on so loudly that people in the front row could hear it over the opening scenes. We apologized, adjusted the thermostat, and restarted the film, but it was still a little distracting. I used to feel that these problems meant we had failed to make a proper event. Now i think the way we respond is part of what people see. We can be embarrassed and still be kind to one another; we can fix what we can and acknowledge what we cannot fix that night.

The room also brings together people who might otherwise only recognize each other from the queue at the pharmacy or from walking dogs on the same street. A retired teacher named Dev often brings a notebook and writes down the titles people mention. A student from the flats across the road once came alone, then returned the next month with her brother. Ruth remembers who prefers a chair near the aisle, while Martin knows which neighbor needs the sound turned down a little. These are small pieces of knowledge, but they make the gathering feel less like a program and more like something shared.

I am not sure the film nights have changed the neighborhood in any large way, and i would not want to claim that they have solved anyone’s loneliness. What i can say is that people now ask when the next screening is, and that the hall feels different to me when it is full. I like the ordinary signs of the evening: someone carrying a mug carefully down the stairs, the pencil note about the extension lead, and the brief pause before the projector starts. When the lights go down, we are still a group of people in a basement room, with coats on the backs of chairs and the last bus approaching. Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "i used the barcode scanning setup during a morning receiving shift, and my overall experience was mixed. the handheld unit felt solid, though the strap sat awkwardly over my glove and i had to adjust it a few times. the home screen was easy enough to read, but getting from the receiving menu to the damaged-label option took more taps than i expected.

most cartons scanned on the first try when their labels were flat and clean. with labels wrapped around corners, i had to tilt the scanner and try again, and the bright warehouse lights made a few glossy labels harder to read. the beep was clear even when the loading area was noisy, which helped me tell when a scan had registered without looking down each time.

when a barcode would not scan, the unit put the carton in an exception queue. i could return to that list later, but the reason field was small and took some careful tapping with gloves on. the connection also paused briefly near the far end of receiving, so i waited there for the screen to update before moving on. i liked that the scan history showed the carton numbers in order. for me, the setup worked best with ordinary, undamaged labels; the awkward strap and the extra steps for exceptions made the rest less smooth.", "output": "I used the barcode scanning setup during a morning receiving shift, and my overall experience was mixed. The handheld unit felt solid, although the strap sat awkwardly over my glove, and I had to adjust it a few times. The home screen was easy enough to read, but getting from the receiving menu to the damaged-label option took more taps than I expected.

Most cartons scanned on the first try when their labels were flat and clean. For labels wrapped around corners, I had to tilt the scanner and try again. The bright warehouse lights also made a few glossy labels harder to read. The beep was clear even when the loading area was noisy, which helped me tell when a scan had registered without looking down each time.

When a barcode would not scan, the unit put the carton in an exception queue. I could return to that list later, but the reason field was small and took careful tapping with gloves on. The connection also paused briefly near the far end of receiving, so I waited for the screen to update before moving on. I liked that the scan history showed the carton numbers in order. For me, the setup worked best with ordinary, undamaged labels; the awkward strap and extra steps for exceptions made the rest less smooth."}]
